facts: A story premise is “a character in a setting with a problem.” [Story Grid, “How to Write a Novel”]
A premise can be phrased as a “what if” question; the article illustrates this with a person stranded on Mars. [Story Grid, “How to Write a Novel”]
Egri says a well-constructed premise contains character, conflict, and conclusion. [Lajos Egri, The Art of Dramatic Writing]

sources.label: Story Grid, “How to Write a Novel”
sources.page: Your Story Idea; The story premise

sources.label: Lajos Egri, The Art of Dramatic Writing

facts: Snowflake Step 1 asks for a one-sentence novel summary, preferably fewer than 15 words. [Randy Ingermanson, “The Snowflake Method For Designing A Novel”]
Ingermanson advises omitting character names and stating who has most to lose and what they want to win. [Randy Ingermanson, “The Snowflake Method For Designing A Novel”]

sources.label: Randy Ingermanson, “The Snowflake Method For Designing A Novel”

facts: Lee Child advises asking or implying a question at the story’s beginning and delaying its answer. [Lee Child, “A Simple Way to Create Suspense”]
The crisis creates a binary choice/question, and the climax is the active answer to the question raised by that crisis. [Story Grid, “The Five Commandments of Storytelling”]

sources.label: Lee Child, “A Simple Way to Create Suspense”
Story Grid, “The Five Commandments of Storytelling”

facts: Maass’s personal-stakes exercise repeatedly asks what would make the protagonist’s problem matter more—ultimately “more than life itself.” [Donald Maass, “Exercise: Defining Personal Stakes”]
His public-stakes exercise starts with the overt, outward conflict, then escalates what would make it worse and imagines failure. [Donald Maass, “Exercise: Raising Public Stakes”]
Bell groups stakes under physical, professional, and psychological death. [James Scott Bell, “High Stakes? Death. Always Death” interview]

facts: Physical death stakes mean that one or many people will die if the antagonistic forces prevail; Bell cites the thriller and The Hunger Games. [James Scott Bell, “High Stakes? Death. Always Death” interview]

facts: Professional death puts a character’s job or vocation on the line; failure can end or seriously damage that part of life. [James Scott Bell, “High Stakes? Death. Always Death” interview]

facts: Psychological death concerns an inner transformation: if the character cannot meet the challenge, they “die inside.” [James Scott Bell, “High Stakes? Death. Always Death” interview]

facts: Sanderson’s plot framework has Promise, Progress, and Payoff: promise creates expectations, progress gives meaningful advancement, and payoff gives a surprising but fulfilling answer. [Brandon Sanderson, “2025 Guide to Plot (Lecture #2)”]
Chekhov’s letter cautions against placing a loaded gun onstage unless someone intends to fire it, a classic setup/payoff rule. [Anton Chekhov, Letter to A. S. Lazarev-Gruzinsky]

sources.page: The Plot Framework: Promise, Progress, and Payoff

facts: Forster distinguishes story from plot by causality: “the king died and then the queen died” is story, while the queen dying of grief is plot; story asks “and then?” and plot asks “why?” [E. M. Forster, Aspects of the Novel]
Stone and Parker advise putting “therefore” or “but,” not “and then,” between beats so the beats carry causation. [Matt Stone and Trey Parker, NYU writing-advice clip]

facts: Weiland’s three-act timing guide places Act I in the first 25%, Act II from about 25% to 75% with a midpoint near 50%, and Act III from about 75% to the end. [K.M. Weiland, “Quick Guide to Timing Plot Points Within Your Story’s Structure”]
Weiland notes novel timing is flexible: a midpoint may land a couple dozen pages on either side of 50%. [K.M. Weiland, “Quick Guide to Timing Plot Points Within Your Story’s Structure”]

sources.label: K.M. Weiland, “Quick Guide to Timing Plot Points Within Your Story’s Structure”

facts: Brody’s first-half beats are Opening Image (0–1%), Theme Stated (5%), Setup (1–10%), Catalyst (10%), Debate (10–20%), Break into Two (20%), and B Story (22%). [Jessica Brody, Save the Cat! Writes a Novel Starter Kit]

The back half is Fun and Games (20–50%), Midpoint (50%), Bad Guys Close In (50–75%), All Is Lost (75%), Dark Night of the Soul (75–80%), Break into Three (80%), Finale (80–99%), and Final Image (99–100%). [Jessica Brody, Save the Cat! Writes a Novel Starter Kit]

sources.label: Jessica Brody, Save the Cat! Writes a Novel Starter Kit

facts: Vogler’s memo lists twelve stages: Ordinary World; Call to Adventure; Refusal; Mentor; Crossing the Threshold; Tests, Allies, Enemies; Approach to the Inmost Cave; Supreme Ordeal; Reward; Road Back; Resurrection; Return with the Elixir. [Christopher Vogler, “A Practical Guide to Joseph Campbell’s The Hero with a Thousand Faces”]

Vogler says the stages may be deleted, added, or reshuffled; the journey is a flexible skeleton rather than a rigid formula. [Christopher Vogler, “A Practical Guide to Joseph Campbell’s The Hero with a Thousand Faces”]

sources.label: Christopher Vogler, “A Practical Guide to Joseph Campbell’s The Hero with a Thousand Faces”

facts: Wells’s seven points are Hook, Plot Turn I, Pinch I, Midpoint, Pinch II, Plot Turn II, and Resolution. [Dan Wells, “Seven-Point Story Structure” (Writing Excuses 7.41)]

The midpoint changes the characters from reaction to action, Plot Turn II supplies the last information needed, and Wells recommends planning backward from the resolution. [Dan Wells, “Seven-Point Story Structure” (Writing Excuses 7.41)]

sources.label: Dan Wells, “Seven-Point Story Structure” (Writing Excuses 7.41)

facts: Freytag’s pyramid has five parts: introduction, rise, climax, return or fall, and catastrophe. [Gustav Freytag, Technique of the Drama, trans. Elias J. MacEwan]
It marks three crises: the exciting force, the tragic force, and the force of last suspense. [Gustav Freytag, Technique of the Drama, trans. Elias J. MacEwan]

sources.label: Gustav Freytag, Technique of the Drama, trans. Elias J. MacEwan
sources.page: ch. II, part 2, Five Parts and Three Crises

facts: Kishōtenketsu names four parts: ki (introduction), shō (development), ten (twist), and ketsu (conclusion). [Shinsuke Tsuchiya, “From Acting Out Stories to Telling Stories”]

Tsuchiya’s table describes ki as orientation, shō as the core narrative, ten as an unexpected development or final key event, and ketsu as interpretation or coda. [Shinsuke Tsuchiya, “From Acting Out Stories to Telling Stories”]

sources.label: Shinsuke Tsuchiya, “From Acting Out Stories to Telling Stories”

facts: A progressive complication follows the inciting incident: habitual tactics fail, each failure raises stakes, and the protagonist must try the next tactic. [Story Grid, “Turning Point Progressive Complication”]
A turning point pushes the protagonist beyond habitual responses into new territory, sets the crisis, and can be active or revelatory. [Story Grid, “Turning Point Progressive Complication”]

sources.label: Story Grid, “Turning Point Progressive Complication”

facts: McKee defines the Inciting Incident as the first major event and primary cause of the following story; it radically upsets the balance of forces in the protagonist’s life. [Robert McKee, Story]

Placement guides differ: Weiland puts the inciting event around 12%, while Brody’s Catalyst is at 10%. [K.M. Weiland, “Quick Guide to Timing Plot Points Within Your Story’s Structure”] [Jessica Brody, Save the Cat! Writes a Novel Starter Kit]

sources.label: Robert McKee, Story
K.M. Weiland, “Quick Guide to Timing Plot Points Within Your Story’s Structure”
Jessica Brody, Save the Cat! Writes a Novel Starter Kit

facts: The climax is the active answer to the question raised by the crisis; it reveals the truth of who the protagonist is under pressure, and the resolution shows the result of that choice. [Story Grid, “The Five Commandments of Storytelling”]
Weiland’s timing guide places the beginning of the climax around 90% of a novel. [K.M. Weiland, “Quick Guide to Timing Plot Points Within Your Story’s Structure”]

sources.label: Story Grid, “The Five Commandments of Storytelling”
K.M. Weiland, “Quick Guide to Timing Plot Points Within Your Story’s Structure”

facts: Reagan et al. analyzed 1,327 Project Gutenberg fiction stories and found six core emotional-arc shapes; an emotional arc measures reader-perceived emotional content, not plot directly. [Andrew J. Reagan et al., “The Emotional Arcs of Stories Are Dominated by Six Basic Shapes”]

The six labels are Rags to riches, Tragedy (Riches to rags), Man in a hole, Icarus, Cinderella, and Oedipus. [Andrew J. Reagan et al., “The Emotional Arcs of Stories Are Dominated by Six Basic Shapes”]

sources.label: Andrew J. Reagan et al., “The Emotional Arcs of Stories Are Dominated by Six Basic Shapes”

facts: “Rags to riches” is the upward emotional arc: a rise in fortune or sentiment. [Andrew J. Reagan et al., “The Emotional Arcs of Stories Are Dominated by Six Basic Shapes”]

sources.label: Andrew J. Reagan et al., “The Emotional Arcs of Stories Are Dominated by Six Basic Shapes”

facts: “Tragedy,” also called “Riches to rags,” is the downward emotional arc. [Andrew J. Reagan et al., “The Emotional Arcs of Stories Are Dominated by Six Basic Shapes”]

sources.label: Andrew J. Reagan et al., “The Emotional Arcs of Stories Are Dominated by Six Basic Shapes”

facts: “Man in a hole” is a fall followed by a rise: the character gets into trouble and then gets out. [Andrew J. Reagan et al., “The Emotional Arcs of Stories Are Dominated by Six Basic Shapes”]

sources.label: Andrew J. Reagan et al., “The Emotional Arcs of Stories Are Dominated by Six Basic Shapes”

facts: “Icarus” is a rise followed by a fall. [Andrew J. Reagan et al., “The Emotional Arcs of Stories Are Dominated by Six Basic Shapes”]

sources.label: Andrew J. Reagan et al., “The Emotional Arcs of Stories Are Dominated by Six Basic Shapes”

facts: “Cinderella” is a rise, fall, and rise again. [Andrew J. Reagan et al., “The Emotional Arcs of Stories Are Dominated by Six Basic Shapes”]

sources.label: Andrew J. Reagan et al., “The Emotional Arcs of Stories Are Dominated by Six Basic Shapes”

facts: “Oedipus” is a fall, rise, and final fall. [Andrew J. Reagan et al., “The Emotional Arcs of Stories Are Dominated by Six Basic Shapes”]

sources.label: Andrew J. Reagan et al., “The Emotional Arcs of Stories Are Dominated by Six Basic Shapes”

facts: In Brody’s Save the Cat model, the B Story starts at 22% and introduces character(s) who help the hero learn the theme, such as a love interest, mentor, friend, or family member. [Jessica Brody, Save the Cat! Writes a Novel Starter Kit]

sources.label: Jessica Brody, Save the Cat! Writes a Novel Starter Kit

facts: MICE is an organizational tool for Milieu, Inquiry, Character, and Event story threads. [Mary Robinette Kowal et al., “What Is the M.I.C.E. Quotient?”]

Stories can contain multiple MICE threads nested like Matryoshka dolls, with each thread opening and closing. [Mary Robinette Kowal et al., “What Is the M.I.C.E. Quotient?”] [Mary Robinette Kowal et al., “Nesting Threads in the M.I.C.E. Quotient”]

sources.label: Mary Robinette Kowal et al., “What Is the M.I.C.E. Quotient?”
Mary Robinette Kowal et al., “Nesting Threads in the M.I.C.E. Quotient”

facts: A Milieu story is driven by a place: it begins when the character enters that place and ends when the character leaves; conflicts delay departure. [Mary Robinette Kowal et al., “What Is the M.I.C.E. Quotient?”]

sources.label: Mary Robinette Kowal et al., “What Is the M.I.C.E. Quotient?”

facts: An Inquiry story begins when a question arises and ends when it is answered; conflicts prevent the protagonist from getting the answer. [Mary Robinette Kowal et al., “What Is the M.I.C.E. Quotient?”]

sources.label: Mary Robinette Kowal et al., “What Is the M.I.C.E. Quotient?”

facts: A Character story starts with dissatisfaction or the question “Who am I?” and ends with recognition or self-definition; conflict blocks the character’s change. [Mary Robinette Kowal et al., “What Is the M.I.C.E. Quotient?”]

sources.label: Mary Robinette Kowal et al., “What Is the M.I.C.E. Quotient?”

facts: An Event story begins when the status quo is disrupted and ends when the old or a new status quo is established; conflict blocks restoration. [Mary Robinette Kowal et al., “What Is the M.I.C.E. Quotient?”]

sources.label: Mary Robinette Kowal et al., “What Is the M.I.C.E. Quotient?”

facts: A try-fail cycle begins when a character tries to solve a problem and fails; the failure creates the next conflict. [Mary Robinette Kowal et al., “Middles and Conflicts with M.I.C.E. Structure”]

The “yes-but” pattern gives a success followed by a complication, while “no-and” gives a failure followed by a worsened situation. [Mary Robinette Kowal et al., “Middles and Conflicts with M.I.C.E. Structure”]

sources.label: Mary Robinette Kowal et al., “Middles and Conflicts with M.I.C.E. Structure”

facts: Scenes are story building blocks that dramatize definable value shifts; their incremental shifts build the global arc of change. [Story Grid, “Units of Story: Beats, Tropes, Scenes, Sequences, and Quadrants”]

sources.label: Story Grid, “Units of Story: Beats, Tropes, Scenes, Sequences, and Quadrants”

facts: Ingermanson’s scene pattern is Goal, Conflict, Disaster; its sequel pattern is Reaction, Dilemma, Decision. [Randy Ingermanson, “Writing The Perfect Scene”]
A disaster is followed by emotional reaction, a dilemma, and a decision that makes the character proactive again and supplies a new scene goal. [Randy Ingermanson, “Writing The Perfect Scene”]

sources.label: Randy Ingermanson, “Writing The Perfect Scene”
sources.page: Large-Scale Structure of a Scene; Motivation-Reaction Units

facts: A scene goal should be specific and clearly definable rather than a vague wish. [Randy Ingermanson, “Writing The Perfect Scene”]

sources.label: Randy Ingermanson, “Writing The Perfect Scene”
sources.page: Large-Scale Structure of a Scene; Motivation-Reaction Units

facts: Scene conflict is the series of obstacles that blocks the viewpoint character from reaching the goal. [Randy Ingermanson, “Writing The Perfect Scene”]

sources.label: Randy Ingermanson, “Writing The Perfect Scene”
sources.page: Large-Scale Structure of a Scene; Motivation-Reaction Units

facts: The scene disaster is failure to reach the goal; Ingermanson warns that simply granting the goal ends the tension and removes a reason to turn the page. [Randy Ingermanson, “Writing The Perfect Scene”]

sources.label: Randy Ingermanson, “Writing The Perfect Scene”
sources.page: Large-Scale Structure of a Scene; Motivation-Reaction Units

facts: The sequel’s reaction is the character’s emotional follow-through after the scene disaster. [Randy Ingermanson, “Writing The Perfect Scene”]

sources.label: Randy Ingermanson, “Writing The Perfect Scene”
sources.page: Large-Scale Structure of a Scene; Motivation-Reaction Units

facts: The sequel’s dilemma presents a situation with no good options, forcing the character to weigh possible responses. [Randy Ingermanson, “Writing The Perfect Scene”]

sources.label: Randy Ingermanson, “Writing The Perfect Scene”
sources.page: Large-Scale Structure of a Scene; Motivation-Reaction Units

facts: The sequel’s decision is the character’s choice of action, restoring a proactive character and establishing the next goal. [Randy Ingermanson, “Writing The Perfect Scene”]

sources.label: Randy Ingermanson, “Writing The Perfect Scene”
sources.page: Large-Scale Structure of a Scene; Motivation-Reaction Units

facts: McKee defines a scene as conflict-driven action that changes a character’s value-charged life condition with perceptible significance. [Robert McKee, “Do Your Scenes Turn?”]
If a scene begins and ends with the same value condition, McKee calls it a nonevent; ideally every scene turns positive to negative or negative to positive. [Robert McKee, “Do Your Scenes Turn?”]

sources.label: Robert McKee, “Do Your Scenes Turn?”

facts: Chekhov’s letter says not to put a loaded gun onstage unless someone intends to fire it, a compact setup/payoff rule. [Anton Chekhov, Letter to A. S. Lazarev-Gruzinsky]
Sanderson frames plot as Promise, Progress, and Payoff: the payoff should be surprising but fulfilling and should honor the core promise. [Brandon Sanderson, “2025 Guide to Plot (Lecture #2)”]

facts: Story Grid describes nested units from beats (smallest unit) and tropes, through scenes, sequences, and quadrants, into a global whole. [Story Grid, “Units of Story: Beats, Tropes, Scenes, Sequences, and Quadrants”]
Each unit is meant to embody the Five Commandments of Storytelling, so local changes accumulate into the global story. [Story Grid, “Units of Story: Beats, Tropes, Scenes, Sequences, and Quadrants”]

facts: A reinforcing feedback loop is amplifying and self-propagating: it enhances whatever direction of change is imposed and can form a virtuous or vicious circle. [UK Government Office for Science, “An introductory systems thinking toolkit for civil servants”]

sources.label: UK Government Office for Science, “An introductory systems thinking toolkit for civil servants”

facts: A balancing feedback loop is stabilising, regulating, and stability-seeking: it opposes whatever direction of change is imposed on the system. [UK Government Office for Science, “An introductory systems thinking toolkit for civil servants”]
